headline: The plastic bag: built to last, used once

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: A bag that won't give out
slides.text: Groceries went home in paper bags. **A Swedish team welded a strong bag from one plastic tube.** The patent named Sten Gustaf Thulin.
slides.alt: Patent drawing of a flat plastic tube with welded seams and punched-out handle shapes, and a finished bag with two handles, signed Inventor Sten Gustaf Thulin
slides.credit: Bag with handle of weldable plastic material, US patent 3,180,557, filed 1962, granted 1965. Sten Gustaf Thulin. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: A penny a bag
slides.text: Rainproof and strong, it caught on. **By 2007 it cost about a penny, paper 4 to 5 cents**, industry figures said.
slides.alt: Two thin peach-colored plastic shopping bags with cut-out handles and a printed fruit design, one flat and one open
slides.credit: Plastic shopping bags, 2011. Phrontis. CC BY-SA 3.0.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Free, so thrown away
slides.statLabel: bags a person a year in Ireland before 2002, a government estimate
slides.text: Handed out free, bags were used once and tossed. **They snagged in trees, blocked drains and drifted out to sea.**
slides.alt: Leafless riverside bushes strung with torn white and blue plastic bags above green water, with round weaverbird nests hanging among them
slides.credit: Plastic bag litter on the Jukskei River, Johannesburg, 2008. NJR ZA. CC BY-SA 3.0.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Partly: the litter was easy to see
slides.text: Litter was easy to see, and in 1972 scientists reported plastic in the open Atlantic. **In 1986 Barry Commoner asked if society really needed plastic bags.**
slides.alt: An ocean sunfish swimming just under the surface of calm blue water, its fin breaking the surface
slides.credit: Ocean sunfish, which feed mainly on jellyfish and can mistake bags for them, Greater Farallones, 2015. NOAA National Marine Sanctuaries. Public domain.

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: A small price, a big drop
slides.text: Ireland's 15 cent levy in 2002 cut use from about 328 bags a person to 21. **By 2018, 127 of 192 countries regulated plastic bags.**

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: A strong, waterproof bag for about a penny, against 4 to 5 cents for paper (industry figures, 2007)
Lower climate impact than a paper bag used fewer than 3 times (UK Environment Agency, 2011)
90% of US grocery bags by 2007, an industry group said
costs: About 5% of Ireland's litter before its 2002 levy (Irish government)
Drains and waterways blocked in Bangladesh, which banned thin bags in 2002
42 billion lightweight bags used in the EU in 2018, about 95 a person (Eurostat)
slides.text: It carried the world's shopping for about a penny a bag. **Given away free, it ended up in trees, drains and the sea.**

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: Great for one, bad for all
slides.text: For each shopper and store, a free bag is the sensible choice. **The cost lands on streets and seas everyone shares.**

slides.label: Lesson
slides.title: A small price can change the total
slides.text: Something built to be reused tends to be used once when it is free. **A small price can change the total.**
